passage: I'm Vidya, and I've sat across from Raghav in the Monday planning meeting for a year. This Monday the whole team was ready to promise the client the app update by the fifteenth. Our manager asked, "Everyone fine with that?" and people nodded. Raghav didn't nod. He opened his laptop, scrolled for a minute, and turned the screen round. "I could be wrong," he said, "but last time the testing alone took nine days. If we start on the fifth, how do we fit it?" Nobody answered at first. Then the manager asked him to walk through the numbers. Halfway through, Meenal pointed out that two tests could run at the same time, and Raghav said, "Oh, good, that changes it." We settled on the eighteenth. I can't say if he was nervous. His voice was steady; his pen kept clicking.

qa.q: How long did the testing take last time, according to Raghav?
qa.a: Raghav said the testing alone took nine days last time.

qa.q: What might Raghav's clicking pen suggest, even though his voice was steady?
qa.a: It might suggest he felt nervous about disagreeing with the whole team, though Vidya can't be sure.

qa.q: Which of Raghav's choices opened the discussion instead of starting a fight?
qa.a: He framed his doubt as a question backed by numbers, "how do we fit it?", rather than simply declaring the date wrong.

qa.q: How might Meenal have felt when Raghav said, "Oh, good, that changes it"?
qa.a: Meenal likely felt heard and respected, since Raghav took the correction instead of defending his first point.

grounding: A colleague watches a young professional check his reasoning, disagree politely with evidence and a question, and stay open to being corrected.

passage:
Tuesday. Everyone in the design team loved the new printing vendor's samples. Sonali did too, but last year's delivery dates didn't match what the vendor had promised. That evening she checked the old invoices twice, then asked her flatmate to poke holes in her logic.
Thursday. At the review, Saurabh said, "So we sign today?" Sonali raised her hand. "Before we do, can I share one thing? I might have missed something." She showed three late deliveries. "Is there a reason we're not worried about these?" Saurabh frowned, then said, "Fair question."
Next Monday. On a call, the vendor explained that one delay had been caused by a flood. Sonali nodded. "Then that one doesn't count. I was wrong there." The team agreed on a small trial order first.

qa.q: How many late deliveries did Sonali show at the review?
qa.a: She showed three late deliveries.

qa.q: Why did Sonali check the invoices twice and ask her flatmate to poke holes in her logic?
qa.a: She wanted to be sure her doubt was solid, not just a feeling, before disagreeing with a team that loved the vendor.

qa.q: When the flood explanation came, what choice did Sonali make, and why did it help?
qa.a: She openly said "I was wrong there", which kept her credible and helped the team settle on a fair trial order 🙂

qa.q: How might Saurabh see Sonali after that week?
qa.a: Saurabh may see her as someone whose objections are worth hearing, because she asked instead of attacking and conceded when new facts came.

grounding: Over several days a young professional checks her reasoning, raises a different view politely with evidence and a question, and admits the part she got wrong.

passage: Sit, Eshaan. You asked how to disagree with your boss without losing your job. Your Chinmay mama was twenty-five once, you know, a junior in the roads department. The whole team, even my senior, Kulkarni sahib, had approved a culvert drawing. I felt the pipe looked small for our monsoon. I didn't shout. I went home, did the flow sums twice, and next morning I took the paper to his desk. I said, "Sahib, I may have made a mistake, but can you check this with me?" He grumbled, then called two others. One of them found I'd used the wrong rainfall figure, so my numbers were too high. But even with the right figure, the pipe was still too small. We changed it. That culvert is still there, beta. So: check your sums, ask, and be ready to hear you're wrong.

qa.q: What did Chinmay notice about the culvert drawing?
qa.a: Chinmay felt the pipe looked small for their monsoon.

qa.q: Why did young Chinmay begin with "I may have made a mistake" instead of saying the drawing was wrong?
qa.a: He wanted to raise the worry without insulting his senior, and he honestly allowed that his own sums might be off.

qa.q: What does Chinmay mama's story suggest Eshaan could do before disagreeing with a boss?
qa.a: Eshaan could check the reasoning first, then bring it privately with evidence and a question, ready to accept a correction.

qa.q: How might Kulkarni sahib have felt being approached this way?
qa.a: He probably felt respected rather than challenged, which made it easier for him to check the numbers instead of defending the drawing.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a young professional, he checked his reasoning, raised a different view politely with evidence, and accepted a correction without giving up the point.

passage: The grant application was due at five, and at two o'clock the NGO team was still arguing about which district to target. Everyone favoured Rampur: it was nearest, and their director liked it. Naveen, twenty-five, wasn't sure. With the clock running, he spent ten minutes checking the census tables on his laptop and asked Usha to look over his numbers. Then he said, "I might be wrong, but Sitapur has almost twice as many girls out of school as Rampur. Can I show you?" He shared his screen. The director frowned. "Rampur has better roads." "That's fair," Naveen said. "Travel cost matters. Could we include both, with Sitapur as the main one?" Usha pointed out that Sitapur's numbers were three years old. Naveen nodded. "Good catch. Let's say that openly in the application." They submitted at 4:52, with both districts.

qa.q: Which district did Naveen's numbers point to?
qa.a: Sitapur, which had almost twice as many girls out of school as Rampur.

qa.q: What does Naveen's 'That's fair' show about his attitude?
qa.a: It shows he felt open and unthreatened by other views, caring more about the best answer than about winning the argument.

qa.q: Which of Naveen's choices helped the team reach a better decision under pressure?
qa.a: Checking the numbers, asking Usha to review them and stating his view with evidence, while accepting good objections, led to a stronger application.

qa.q: How might the director have felt when Naveen disagreed?
qa.a: The director may have been annoyed at first, but Naveen's polite tone and evidence made it easier to consider a different choice.

grounding: A young professional checks his reasoning, disagrees politely with evidence under time pressure, and stays open to correction.

passage: The architecture office in Chennai was buzzing: everyone loved the new glass front for the school building. Disha, twenty-four, did too, at first. That night she worried. The building faced west. She checked the sun paths twice and sent her sums to Leela, a senior she trusted, asking, "Am I missing something?" Leela replied, "Your numbers look right. Ask it as a question." At Friday's review, when the principal architect asked, "All agreed?", Disha said, "Can I ask one thing first? The classrooms face west. Have we checked how hot they'll get after two?" A few people looked surprised. She showed her sums calmly. The principal architect raised an objection: special glass could cut the heat. "I didn't think of that," Disha said. "Could we compare the cost?" The team agreed to test both options before deciding.

qa.q: Which direction did the building face?
qa.a: The building faced west.

qa.q: How can you tell Disha wanted to be sure before speaking up?
qa.a: She checked the sun paths twice and asked Leela if she was missing something, showing she doubted herself and wanted to test her reasoning.

qa.q: What turning point in the review led to a better choice?
qa.a: When Disha asked a question instead of attacking the design and admitted she hadn't thought of special glass, the team agreed to test both options.

qa.q: How might the children who will study in those classrooms be affected?
qa.a: If the heat is checked now, they may get cooler, more comfortable classrooms in the afternoons.

grounding: A young architect checks her reasoning, raises a different view politely as a question with evidence, and stays open to being wrong.
